diagnosticHolds.excerpt: Test the fuel pump relay first as it is a cheaper fix.

Charging: swap to a high-output one-wire 3G Ford alternator (roughly 90A at idle, up to ~130A) and run a NEW heavy-gauge charge wire straight from the alternator to the battery / starter-relay battery post (mandatory over ~70A) instead of through the old harness.
Because the high-output unit bypasses the factory ammeter loop, delete the ammeter and fit a voltmeter that drops into the stock cluster.
Dealers perform engine cycle test under recall.
If the airbag light is on, scan the RCM/SRS system for stored faults before replacing components.
Persistent black-screen or camera failures may require APIM or camera module diagnosis and replacement.

Diagnose per Ford bulletins: SSM 51011 covers hot-slip on 8F35 units built on/before 16-Mar-2022 (remedy is replacing the internal case-half pump seals, part 7N265), and TSB 21-2268 covers the P0766 MIL.
Persistent engagement delays beyond 2 seconds should be diagnosed for possible valve body issues under powertrain warranty.
Typical repair cost ranges from $150-$900 depending on whether the issue is tune-up related or requires deeper diagnosis.
Run Ford's pinpoint test that cycles the solenoid to dislodge debris, then change oil and filter.
If fluid is clean, test the TCC solenoid and wiring and service the fluid.
Test the battery as chronic undercharging may have damaged it.
Diagnose which circuit has lost power (fuel pump, fan, A/C clutch, PCM feed), then replace the CCRM with an OEM-spec matching unit and clean/repair the connector for corrosion.
Diagnose using GEM module DTCs first - many issues are electrical (shift motor or GEM) rather than mechanical.
Some Ford vehicles have a built-in HVAC self-test accessible through the climate control panel.
Diagnose early with a combustion-gas (block) test on the coolant before catastrophic failure.
Test/replace the DPFE sensor (an inexpensive Motorcraft/aftermarket part), clean or replace the EGR valve, and clear the carbon-clogged EGR tube/ports.
Perform an EVAP smoke test to pinpoint the leak;
Perform a key-off parasitic-draw test and pull fuses to isolate the offending module;
Scan the seat modules for stored faults.
Test the primary and auxiliary battery state of health and replace as needed;
Diagnose fluid condition (burnt smell, metal), line pressure, and DTCs before teardown.
Pinpoint the source with a careful water test from the bottom up.
After repair, the SRS light should be cleared and the system rechecked with a capable scan tool.
If the truck still will not start, test the fuel pump and rail pressure sensor circuit next.
Diagnosis usually confirms a failed cable-style window regulator or broken pulley assembly inside the door.
Read freeze-frame and identify the specific cylinder;
Diagnose the boost-control fault and rule out unrelated causes first (charge-pipe/boost leaks, cracked intercooler pipe, BOV, solenoid, vacuum leaks).
Always perform a high-pressure smoke test of the charge-air system before condemning the turbos.
If the leadframe checks out, diagnose the specific companion code (solenoid, valve body, wiring/connector corrosion, or low/burnt fluid).
If the owner simply dislikes the feature, a memory-retaining start-stop disable module keeps it off without affecting the battery diagnosis.
Diagnose with Ford IDS or quality OBDII scanner capable of reading all PCM codes.
Read misfire codes to identify the cylinder.
Have the speed sensors and solenoids tested if shuddering occurs — replacing a $100 sensor is preferable to a $5,000 transmission.
Test vacuum at the booster — should hold 15+ inches of vacuum.
If the transmission begins slipping or stalling, have speed sensors and solenoids tested first ($100-$300 for sensor replacement).
Have the fuel pressure tested under load — a weak fuel pump is the most common cause of stalling and should be replaced ($400-$700 including labor).
Water-test to locate the entry point, then reseal or replace the taillight gaskets/rivet grommets, trunk weatherstrip, and rear-window seal;
Run a properly sized charge cable (8-gauge) straight to the battery and bypass/upgrade the factory ammeter circuit so the higher current isn't pushed through the original undersized wiring.
Rule out upstream misfire/fuel-trim/exhaust-leak causes, then swap-test the Bank 2 downstream O2 sensor with Bank 1.
Diagnose a suspected head gasket with a combustion-gas (block) test or by watching for bubbles in the coolant.
If overheating already occurred, pressure-test for a cracked head/blown head gasket.
Diagnose specifics first: adjust the TV/kickdown cable and service fluid/filter for early slipping;
Many owners repair the cluster by reflowing cracked solder joints at the connector and stepper/gauge board connections, while others replace the cluster with a remanufactured unit.
No diagnostic repair is appropriate other than recall completion with updated parts.
A full cooling-system flush and pressure test should accompany the repair.
erratic or harsh shifting should be diagnosed early before hard-part damage occurs.
Test the battery after alternator replacement - a chronically undercharged battery may have permanent sulfation damage.
Test the battery — a failing battery can cause alternator overwork and premature failure.
Diagnose with Ford IDS/FDRS scan tool to identify BCM fault codes.
If confirmed, replace the steering gear/EPAS rack or related control module per Ford diagnostics and perform steering angle/center calibration.
Diagnose CAN bus communication using Ford IDS/FDRS to identify any U-code network faults.
Leak-test the system, repair/replace leaking rear A/C lines or rear expansion valve seals/components as needed, then evacuate and recharge to specification.
if symptoms persist, diagnose for valve body issues and solenoid performance and service/replace the main control/valve body as directed.
Clearing the fault and re-testing boost response is required after replacement.
Recover and measure refrigerant, leak-test with dye/nitrogen, and repair leaking components (O-rings/lines/condenser as needed).
Scan ABS module for wheel speed sensor DTCs and view live wheel speed data to identify the affected corner.
Diagnose for exhaust leaks, misfires, and fuel trim issues before replacing parts.
Scan for misfire counters and DTCs, then replace the failed ignition coil(s);
After replacement, a steering angle sensor calibration must be performed with a Ford IDS or compatible scan tool.
Pull back the hinge/boot and perform a continuity test on suspect circuits;
